Now, we're going to use linear regression to fit a line to the trend, which looks almost linear, and use fourier curves to fit to the seasonal component;

In [4]:
def plot_periodogram(ts, detrend='linear', ax=None):
    from scipy.signal import periodogram
    fs = pd.Timedelta("365D") / pd.Timedelta("1D")
    freqencies, spectrum = periodogram(
        ts,
        fs=fs,
        detrend=detrend,
        window="boxcar",
        scaling='spectrum',
    )
    if ax is None:
        _, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.step(freqencies, spectrum, color="purple")
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set_xticks([1, 2, 4, 6, 12, 26, 52, 104])
    ax.set_xticklabels(
        [
            "Annual (1)",
            "Semiannual (2)",
            "Quarterly (4)",
            "Bimonthly (6)",
            "Monthly (12)",
            "Biweekly (26)",
            "Weekly (52)",
            "Semiweekly (104)",
        ],
        rotation=30,
    )
    ax.ticklabel_format(axis="y", style="sci", scilimits=(0, 0))
    ax.set_ylabel("Variance")
    ax.set_title("Periodogram")
    return ax

plot_periodogram(data.Prices)

The Periodogram shows an annual seasonality, so, we apply the fourier as such:

In [5]:
fourier = CalendarFourier(freq="YE", order=6)  # I'm using order 6 to get enough complexity without overfitting to the data

data_train, data_test = train_test_split(data, shuffle = False, test_size = 0.2)

dp = DeterministicProcess(
    index=data_train.index,
    constant=True,               # dummy feature for bias (y-intercept)
    order=1,                     # trend (order 1 means linear)
    seasonal=True,
    additional_terms=[fourier],  # annual seasonality (fourier)
    drop=True,                   # drop terms to avoid collinearity
)

X_train = dp.in_sample()  # create features for dates in data.index
y_train = data_train["Prices"]

model = LinearRegression(fit_intercept=False)
_ = model.fit(X_train, y_train)

X_test = dp.out_of_sample(steps = len(data_test))

y_train_fit = pd.Series(model.predict(X_train), index=X_train.index)
y_test = pd.Series(model.predict(X_test), index=X_test.index)

ax = y_train.plot(color='0.25', style="--", title="Natural Gas Stores - Seasonal Forecast")
ax = y_train_fit.plot(ax=ax, label="Prediction")
ax = y_test.plot(ax=ax, label="Forecast")
_ = ax.legend()

plt.show();

JPMorgan Chase & Co. QR Job Sim - Task 2¶

Let's load our data and model from the last task;

In [10]:
"""
Natural Gas Price Forecasting
"""

### IMPORTS
import pandas as pd
from datetime import datetime
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from statsmodels.tsa.deterministic import CalendarFourier, DeterministicProcess
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

### DATA PRE-PROCESSING

# Reading data from csv stored in "sheets/Nat_Gas.csv"
data = pd.read_csv("sheets/Nat_Gas.csv")

# Applying datetime filter over "Dates" column
data["Dates"] = data["Dates"].apply(lambda x : datetime.strptime(x, "%m/%d/%y"))

# Converting index to Datetime format
data = data.set_index(data["Dates"])

# Removing Dates column
data = data.drop("Dates", axis=1)

# Increasing granularity by resampling data to daily and using linear interpolation to fill in gaps
data = data.resample("1D").asfreq()
data = data.interpolate(method = "linear")

### MODELLING

# Using order 6 to get enough complexity without overfitting to the data
fourier = CalendarFourier(freq="YE", order=6)  

# Setting process
dp = DeterministicProcess(
    index=data.index,
    constant=True,
    order=1,
    seasonal=True,
    additional_terms=[fourier],
    drop=True
)

# Create features for dates in data.index and setting target y
X = dp.in_sample() 
y = data["Prices"]

# Training lin-reg model to data
model = LinearRegression(fit_intercept=False)
_ = model.fit(X, y)

# Forecasting 365 steps (1 year)
X_fore = dp.out_of_sample(steps = 365)

# Fitting model
y_fit = pd.Series(model.predict(X), index=X.index)
y_fore = pd.Series(model.predict(X_fore), index=X_fore.index)

# Making final prediction dataset
full_pred = pd.concat([y_fit, y_fore], join = "inner")

### OUTPUTS

# Input management
#userinput = str(input("Please input a date in the form mm/dd/yy :\n"))

#userinput = datetime.strptime(userinput, "%m/%d/%y")

#print(full_pred.loc[userinput])

We want to make a function that takes inputs:

  • Injection dates - we use $t$ to denote the date, $I$ to indicate the number of injections and $V_{I,t}$ to indicate injection volume in millions.
  • Withdrawal dates - we use $t$ to denote the date, $W$ to indicate the number of withdrawals and $V_{W,t}$ to indicate withdrawal volume in millions.
  • The prices at which the commodity can be purchased/sold on those dates $B_t$, $S_t$ (buy, sell) - based on our pricing model from task 1.
  • The rate at which the gas can be injected/withdrawn $r_I$, $r_W$ million MMBtu per transaction.
  • The cost of injecting and withdrawing $P_I$, $P_W$ per million MMBtu.
  • The maximum volume that can be stored $V$.
  • Storage costs $C$
  • The duration of time in months between the first injection and final withdrawal $T$

And prices a contract according to some algorithm.

Let's go by the following equations to price our model: $$ P = \left(\sum (S_t - P_WV_{W,t}) - \sum (B_t - P_IV_{I,t})\right) - C T $$ $$ r_I \geq V_{I,t}\hspace{10mm} r_W \geq V_{W,t} $$ $$ V \geq \sum^t_\tau V_{I,\tau} - \sum^t_\tau V_{W,\tau} \hspace{10mm} \forall t $$

In [11]:
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
import numpy as np
import math

# A function that takes parameters Injection/Withdrawal dates, amounts, rate and cost, Maximum Volume, Cost of storage, and prediction model results
def price_contract(InjectionDates, WithdrawalDates, InjectionAmount, WithdrawalAmount, InjectRate, WithdrawRate, InjectCost, WithdrawCost, MaxVol, StoreCost, prediction):
    # Set Contract Price variable
    ContractPrice = 0

    # Sort injection prices and amounts into a dataframe
    InjectionPrices = prediction[InjectionDates]
    WithdrawalPrices = prediction[WithdrawalDates]

    Injections = pd.concat([InjectionPrices, pd.Series(InjectionAmount, index = InjectionPrices.index)], axis = 1)
    Injections.columns = ["Injection Price", "Injection Amount"]

    Withdrawals = pd.concat([WithdrawalPrices, pd.Series(WithdrawalAmount, index = WithdrawalPrices.index)], axis = 1)
    Withdrawals.columns = ["Withdrawal Price", "Withdrawal Amount"]

    Operations = pd.concat([Injections, Withdrawals], axis = 1)

    # Set variables for how much gas is stored, and the change in value per transaction
    stored = 0
    value = []

    # This loop handles dealing with how much gas is in storage, how much we spend and earn, and handle potential errors
    for date in Operations.index:

        # Choosing the entry
        entry = Operations.loc[date]
        entry = entry.drop(entry[entry.isna()].index)
        
        # If the entry is an injection
        if entry.index.any() == "Injection Price":

            # If we're trying to inject more than allowed
            if entry["Injection Amount"] > InjectRate:
                return("Injection Error : Injection Amount greater than allowed rate")
            
            # If we have enough space to inject
            elif stored <= (MaxVol - entry["Injection Amount"]):
                stored += entry["Injection Amount"] # Add to storage
                value.append(-1 * (entry["Injection Price"] * entry["Injection Amount"] + InjectCost * (entry["Injection Amount"]/1000000))) # We spend : price*amount + cost*amount/mil

            # If we don't have enough space to inject
            else:
                return("Injection Error : Out of storage")
            
        # If the entry is a withdrawal
        else:
            # If we try to withdraw more than allowed
            if entry["Withdrawal Amount"] > WithdrawRate:
                return("Withdraw Error : Withdrawal Amount greater than allowed rate")
            
            # If we have enough gas to withdraw
            elif entry["Withdrawal Amount"] <= stored:
                stored -= entry["Withdrawal Amount"] # Remove from storage
                value.append(entry["Withdrawal Price"] * entry["Withdrawal Amount"] - WithdrawCost * (entry["Withdrawal Amount"]/1000000)) # We earn : price*amount - cost*amount/mil

            # If we try to withdraw more than we have
            else:
                return("Withdrawal Error : Out of storage")
            
    # Calculate the price of the contract
    timeelapsed = math.ceil((Operations.index[-1] - Operations.index[0]).days/30)
    ContractPrice = np.array(value).sum() - (StoreCost * timeelapsed)

    return(ContractPrice)

#Example input
Inj = [datetime(2024, 9, 30), datetime(2024, 10, 2), datetime(2024, 10, 12), datetime(2024, 10, 15)]
With = [datetime(2024, 12, 10), datetime(2024, 12, 30)]

InjAm = [5000000, 5000000, 5000000, 5000000]
WithAm = [15000000, 5000000]

price = price_contract(Inj, With, InjAm, WithAm, 5000000, 100000000, 10000, 10000, 50000000, 100000, full_pred)

print(price)

By intuition, I also think all of the columns might be relevant to whether the customer defaults - but I'll replace payment, debt and income with payment/income and debt/income.

Perfect - it seems we have a pretty strong model, now, we need to make a function to take features as input and return the expected loss on the loan.

In [16]:
# Function takes all important features as input
def exploss(creditlines, loanamt, debtamt, income, employedyears, fico, model):
    
    # Creates customer profile
    information = [creditlines, debtamt/income, loanamt/income, employedyears, fico]
    customer = pd.DataFrame(information)
    customer = customer.transpose()
    customer.columns = ['credit_lines_outstanding', 'debt_to_income', 'loan_to_income', 'years_employed', 'fico_score']

    # Get probability of defaulting
    probdefault = (model.predict_proba(customer)[0][1])

    # We use recov rate 0.1
    recov = 0.1
    LGD = (1-0.1) * loanamt
    ExpectedLoss = LGD * probdefault
    return(ExpectedLoss)

Now, we need to make a rating map - where lower rating signifies better credit score - we'll make 5 buckets from 0 - 600 and 5 buckets from 600 - 850.

We will always try to maximise the log-likelihood function as our indication of well optimised.

In [18]:
from optbinning import OptimalBinning

def loglike(n, k, b):
    n = np.array(n)
    k = np.array(k)
    b = np.array(b)

    p = k/n
    
    loglikelihood = (k * np.log(p) + (n - k) * np.log(1-p)).sum()

    return(loglikelihood)


variable = "fico_score"
x = data[variable].values
y = data.default

optb = OptimalBinning(name=variable, dtype="numerical")

optb.fit(x, y)

bins = optb.splits
bins = np.append(bins, np.array([850]))
bins = np.append(np.array([0]), bins)

labels = np.arange(len(bins)-1, 0, -1)

data["rating"] = pd.cut(data["fico_score"], bins = bins, labels = labels)

data.sort_values("fico_score")
